title.en: Meet me at the 7th shop in the 5th row

text.en: Imagine you tell a friend, meet me at the 7th shop in the 5th row from the entrance of the market. Two numbers are enough to find one shop among hundreds. The whole Earth can be searched in the same way, with two numbers for every place. In this chapter we learn how a map works, how latitude and longitude give two numbers for any place, and why clocks in different countries show different times.

Imagine that you get off a train in a city you have never visited. You want to find the bank, the school, the museum and the public garden. You could ask someone, or you could read a map. A map is a drawing of some area as if you were looking at it from straight above. The area may be small like a village, bigger like a district or a state, or very large like India or the whole world. The textbook calls a map a treasure guide, because it shows where things are and how to reach them. A book or collection of maps is called an atlas. There are different kinds of maps. Physical maps show natural features such as mountains, oceans and rivers. Political maps show countries or states, their boundaries, cities and capitals. Thematic maps show one special kind of information, for example where crops grow.
Every map has three important components: distance, direction and symbols. Distance is shown by the scale. A huge place fits on a small sheet because each centimetre on the map stands for a fixed distance on the ground. If the scale is 1 cm equals 500 m, then 3 cm on the map means 1500 m on the ground. On the map of India in Chapter 5, the scale is a small ruler marked 500 km. That ruler is 2.5 cm long in the printed map, so every 2.5 cm stands for 500 kilometres. For direction, a map shows four cardinal directions: north at the top, then east, south and west going clockwise. Between them are the intermediate directions northeast, southeast, southwest and northwest. Most maps simply carry an arrow marked N that points to the north. Symbols are small signs for roads, railway lines, rivers, wells, temples, post offices, police stations and trees. A large city or a country has no space to draw every building, so a symbol stands for each kind of feature.
Mapping the Earth is harder because our planet is not flat. It is nearly a sphere. We say nearly because it is slightly flattened at the poles, but in practice we treat it as a sphere. You cannot show a sphere perfectly on flat paper. Peel an orange so that the skin comes off in three or four big pieces, then try to flatten them on a table. They tear at the edges. A globe is a sphere with a map drawn on it. Because the globe has the same shape as the Earth, it shows the geography of the Earth better than any flat map.
The market shop and the chessboard square show the idea of coordinates. On a chessboard the columns are letters a to h and the rows are numbers 1 to 8. A pawn that moves from d2 to d4 has a start and an end, each fixed by one letter and one number. Maps use the same idea. A place on the Earth is fixed by two coordinates, which are called latitude and longitude.
Find the North Pole and the South Pole on a globe. They stay fixed when you spin the globe. Halfway between them is the Equator. If you stand on the Equator and walk towards a pole, your distance from the Equator grows. Latitude measures this distance. A line that runs east to west, parallel to the Equator, is called a parallel of latitude, and each one makes a circle around the Earth. The Equator is the biggest circle. The circles get smaller as you go north or south. Latitude is measured in degrees. The Equator is 0 degrees, and the two poles are 90 degrees North and 90 degrees South. Latitude is linked to climate. Near the Equator it is generally hot, which is called torrid. Moving towards the poles the climate becomes moderate or temperate. Close to the poles it becomes cold, called frigid.
Now imagine travelling from the North Pole to the South Pole by the shortest line. You could pass through Europe and Africa, or through Asia, and the distance would be the same. These half circles from pole to pole are called meridians of longitude. To measure longitude we need a starting line. The Prime Meridian passes through Greenwich, a part of London in England. In 1884 some nations agreed to make it the international standard, and it is marked 0 degrees longitude. It is also called the Greenwich Meridian. Longitude measures the distance from the Prime Meridian along the Equator, in degrees from 0 to 180, east or west. New York is about 74 degrees West, Delhi about 77 degrees East and Tokyo about 140 degrees East. The line 180 degrees East and 180 degrees West is the same line. Latitude and longitude together are the two coordinates of a place. For example, Delhi lies at about 29 degrees North and 77 degrees East. Together, the parallels and meridians form a grid on the globe. The Prime Meridian splits the Earth into the Western and Eastern Hemispheres. The Equator splits it into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. India had a prime meridian long before Europe. It was called madhya rekha, the middle line, and passed through Ujjayini, which is today Ujjain. Varahamihira, a famous astronomer, worked there about 1500 years ago. India itself lies roughly between 8 degrees North and 37 degrees North in latitude, and between 68 degrees East and 97 degrees East in longitude.
The Earth spins from west to east and makes a full turn of 360 degrees in 24 hours. So it turns 15 degrees every hour, because 15 times 24 is 360. Because of this, when it is morning in one country it is lunchtime in another and night in a third. Measuring the longitude of a place also tells us its time. Starting at the Prime Meridian, every 15 degrees to the east adds one hour. If it is 12 noon at Greenwich, it is 1 pm at 15 degrees East and 2 pm at 30 degrees East. Going west it is the other way: 11 am at 15 degrees West and 10 am at 30 degrees West. Think of two friends on the phone, one in Porbandar in Gujarat and the other in Tinsukia in Assam. In Assam the Sun has already set, but in Gujarat it is still daylight. Taking the difference in longitude to be 30 degrees, their local times differ by 2 hours.
The time worked out from the longitude of your own place is the local time. It would be very confusing for a country to use many local times, so most countries adopt one standard time based on a meridian that passes through them. Indian Standard Time is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich Mean Time, written GMT. So when it is 12 noon in London, it is 5.30 in the evening in India. Standard times are arranged in time zones that broadly follow the 15 degree strips. The zone lines are not perfectly straight, because they follow the borders of countries. Numbers written on a world map tell how many hours to add to GMT, or subtract if the sign is negative. Very large countries may need more than one zone. The USA has six time zones and Russia has eleven. Travelling across Russia from east to west, you would reset your watch ten times. The line opposite the Prime Meridian, at about 180 degrees, is called the International Date Line. The plus 12 and minus 12 time zones touch here. Crossing it eastward you subtract a day, and crossing it westward you add a day. The line bends in places so that a country is not split into two different days.

problem.en: Two clocks, one moment: the time at 45 degrees East when it is 12 noon at Greenwich

text.en: Find how far 45 degrees East is from Greenwich.

why.en: Greenwich is at 0 degrees, so the difference is 45 degrees.

text.en: Divide by 15 degrees per hour.
East means ahead, so add 3 hours to 12 noon.

why.en: Going east adds time, so the local time is 3 pm.

problem.en: A playground is 40 m by 30 m. On a scale of 1 cm = 10 m, how long is its diagonal in real life?

text.en: Draw it on the scale.

why.en: The sides become 4 cm and 3 cm.

text.en: Measure the diagonal on the drawing.

why.en: It measures 5 cm, as in a 3, 4, 5 triangle.

text.en: Multiply by the scale.

why.en: 5 cm times 10 m is 50 m on the ground.

prompt.en: Explain, in your own words, how latitude and longitude help us find a place and why clocks differ across the world.

requiredIdeas.en: Latitude is the distance from the Equator in degrees and longitude is the distance from the Prime Meridian
A place is fixed by two numbers, its latitude and longitude
The Earth turns 15 degrees each hour so every 15 degrees of longitude is one hour
Standard time is used inside a country and India is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking the Equator is a line of longitude
Thinking the Earth is a perfect sphere
Thinking every country has just one time zone

points.en: A map shows an area from above. Its components are distance (scale), direction and symbols.
The Earth is nearly a sphere, so a globe shows it better than a flat map.
Latitude (parallels, east to west) and longitude (meridians, pole to pole) are the two coordinates of a place.
The Equator is 0 degrees latitude and the Prime Meridian at Greenwich is 0 degrees longitude.
The Earth turns 15 degrees every hour, so 15 degrees of longitude equals one hour. IST is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.
The International Date Line lies near 180 degrees: cross it going east and you lose a day, going west you gain one.
